n: Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, hears about Jericho and Ai — and that nearby Gibeon has made peace with Israel. His name, “my lord is righteous,” recalls Melchizedek, an earlier righteous king of Salem.

f.g: “My lord is righteousness.”

n: This alarmed him greatly: Gibeon was a major, well-defended city with strong fighters. Its defection opened the road into the hills.

f.g: As important as a city with a king.

n: He calls four other southern kings to join him: Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

f.g: Where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried.
A major fortified city in the lowlands.

n: “Help me punish Gibeon for siding with Israel.”

f.g: Attack Gibeon.

n: The five Amorite kings unite and besiege Gibeon.

f.w: the five kings of the Amorites
f.g: “Amorite” here broadly means the hill-country peoples.

n: Gibeon sends an urgent plea to Joshua: “Don’t abandon your servants — come quickly!” The treaty, though gained by deception, now obligates Israel to defend them.

f.g: Don’t withdraw your help.

n: Joshua marches out from Gilgal with his whole army. Israel honors its covenant even toward those who tricked them.

f.g: Gilgal is in the low Jordan valley; Gibeon is high in the hills — a steep climb.

n: God reassures Joshua: Don’t fear — I have already handed them to you.
Joshua marches uphill all night — about 20 miles (30 km) — and launches a surprise attack.

f.w: went up from Gilgal all night
f.g: A forced night march.

n: The Lord throws the enemy into panic. Israel chases them along the pass of Beth-horon toward Azekah and Makkedah.

f.g: Threw into confusion and panic.
A key mountain pass leading down to the lowlands.

n: As they flee, God sends huge hailstones that kill more than Israel’s swords. The battle clearly belongs to the Lord.
Joshua prays boldly before Israel: “Sun, stand still over Gibeon; Moon, over the valley of Aijalon.” He asks for more time to complete the victory.

f.w: Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon

f.g: Aijalon, a valley west of Gibeon.

n: The sun stopped for about a full day. The account quotes the Book of Jasher, an ancient collection now lost. Mormon later reflected that it is the earth that moves, not the sun — God controls both.

f.g: “The Book of the Upright,” a lost ancient poetic record.

n: A unique day: never before or since did God so respond to a man’s voice, because he fought for Israel.

f.w: the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man

n: A summary note that Israel later returned to Gilgal; the story then backs up to tell what happened to the five kings.

f.g: This verse anticipates verse 43.

n: The five kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah.

f.g: A town in the lowlands, location uncertain.

n: Joshua is told where they are hiding.

f.g: Discovered hiding.

n: Joshua seals the cave with large stones and posts guards — dealing with the kings later.

f.w: set men by it for to keep them
f.g: Station guards.

n: Priority: pursue the fleeing armies before they reach their walled cities.

f.g: Attack their rear guard.
Don’t allow them.

n: Israel inflicts a heavy defeat; survivors reach their fortified cities.

f.g: Walled, fortified cities.

n: The army returns safely to Joshua. No one dared even speak against Israel.

f.g: An idiom: no one dared to threaten them.

n: Joshua orders the cave opened and the five kings brought out.

f.w: Open the mouth of the cave
f.g: Remove the stones.

n: The kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon are presented.
Joshua has his commanders place their feet on the kings’ necks — an ancient symbol of total victory.

f.w: put your feet upon the necks of these kings

n: Joshua passes on God’s own encouragement: don’t fear — this is what the Lord will do to all your enemies.

f.w: be strong and of good courage

n: The kings are executed and their bodies hung on trees until evening.
At sunset, as the law required, the bodies were taken down and sealed in the same cave they had hidden in.

f.w: at the time of the going down of the sun

n: Makkedah is taken that same day, and its king treated like Jericho’s.

f.g: Under the ban (ḥerem).

n: The campaign moves on to Libnah.

f.g: A lowland city, later a Levitical city.

n: God gives Libnah and its king into Israel’s hand as well.

f.g: The narrator repeatedly credits God, not Israel.

n: Next is Lachish, a powerful fortress city.

f.g: Besieged it.

n: Lachish falls on the second day.

f.g: A strong city needed a two-day siege.

n: Horam, king of Gezer, comes to help Lachish but is defeated. (Gezer itself was not captured; it remained Canaanite until Solomon’s time.)
Then on to Eglon.

f.g: A lowland city near Lachish.

n: Eglon is taken in one day.

f.g: Rapid success.

n: The army climbs into the hill country to Hebron.

f.g: Hebron lies high in the Judean hills.

n: Hebron and its surrounding towns are taken. Later, Caleb had to drive out the giants still living there, showing that the conquest happened in stages.

f.g: The villages and towns dependent on Hebron.

n: Then Debir, southwest of Hebron.

f.g: Also called Kirjath-sepher, “city of the book.”

n: Debir is taken as well. Its later recapture by Othniel shows that Canaanites sometimes resettled conquered sites.

f.w: as he had done to Hebron, so he did to Debir

n: A sweeping summary: hill country, the southern desert, the lowlands, and the slopes. The narrator uses idealized language; later chapters and Judges show much land still unconquered.

f.g: The Negev desert.
The slopes descending toward the Dead Sea.

f.w: as the LORD God of Israel commanded

n: From Kadesh-barnea in the far south to Gaza on the coast, and from the region of Goshen up to Gibeon.

f.g: A region in southern Judah — not the Goshen in Egypt.

n: All in one campaign — because the Lord fought for Israel. That is the chapter’s main point.

f.w: the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel

n: Joshua and the army return to their base at Gilgal.
